paragraphs.text: This is [Wuyi rock tea](yancha:definition), the oolong of the [Wuyi Mountains](wuyi-mountains:where-it-is) on the border of northern Fujian and Jiangxi, and only tea from that area may be sold under the name. The bushes grow among rock, on ledges and in the ravines, in [thin soil weathered from the cliffs](wuyi-mountains:nature) that drains fast while fog settles on the slopes through the year. The record names no zone or pit, so it does not say how close to the [scenic core](wuyi-mountains:zones) this leaf grew.

Like any [oolong](oolong:definition), it is only partly oxidised. The leaf is twisted into long strips rather than rolled into balls, then finished with a [charcoal roast](yancha:making) given in several rounds, with rests of weeks or months between them. The roast dries the tea so it keeps, and the roaster matches its strength to the leaf in hand.

brewing.text: Wuyi tea is usually brewed gongfu style with water at or near the boil, about 95 to 100°C, and about 5 to 8 grams of leaf in a 100 to 120 ml gaiwan, a third to a half full. A quick rinse, poured off at once, is common. Steeps start short, about 5 to 20 seconds, and grow a few seconds longer each round, and good rock tea gives seven steeps or more. In a larger pot, use about 2 to 5 grams for 250 to 350 ml and steep two to three minutes.

notice.text: Roast and stone fruit, a mineral, rocky texture and a long, sweet, mouth-watering finish. Light roast is bright and floral, medium roast fruity and rounded, full roast charcoal, wood and roasted nuts. Da Hong Pao is often floral, Rougui spicy with cinnamon, young Shui Xian sweet and smooth, and old-bush Shui Xian woody and mossy.
